terms.gloss: go to one’s work, one’s post
terms.grammar: ad with the accusative of officium; also with proficīscī
evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.5.9: ante lūcem ībat ad Vespasiānum imperātōrem … inde ad dēlēgātum sibi officium
terms.comment: Pliny’s words for his uncle’s working day: before dawn to the emperor, then to the post entrusted to him, then home to his books. Officium is the duty or the post itself, not the room where it is done (for that see “office”), so the phrase serves whether the work is in town or in the study at home.

evidence: Cic. Quinct. 19: quī ad negōtium suum relictō prōcūrātōre proficīscuntur

phrases.latin: Ante lūcem ībat ad Vespasiānum imperātōrem … inde ad dēlēgātum sibi officium. Reversus domum quod reliquum temporis studiīs reddēbat.
phrases.english: Before dawn he went to the emperor Vespasian … and from there to the work assigned to him. When he got home, he gave what was left of his time to his studies.

phrases.latin: numquam tam māne ēgredior neque tam vesperī domum revortor quīn tē in fundō cōnspicer fodere aut arāre aut aliquid ferre dēnique
phrases.english: I never go out so early or come home so late in the evening that I don’t see you on your farm, digging or ploughing or at least carrying something.

phrases.latin: Pater ad officium it; vesperī domum revertētur.
phrases.english: Daddy’s going to work; he’ll be home this evening.
When I’ve finished work, I’ll play with you.

sources: Lewis & Short: officium · Lewis & Short: eo · Lewis & Short: proficiscor · Lewis & Short: negotium
